title: THE PSALM THAT REVEALS WHAT DEPRESSION FEELS LIKE
paragraphs: THE PSALM THAT REVEALS WHAT DEPRESSION FEELS LIKE
There are chapters in life that nobody posts about.
The nights when the room is quiet but your mind is loud.
The mornings when getting out of bed feels heavier than carrying stones.
The moments when you smile in public and collapse in private.
The days when people ask, “How are you?” and you answer, “Fine,” because explaining the truth would take too long.
And many feel guilty for them.
They wonder if real Christians should feel this way.
Yet hidden in Scripture is a psalm so raw, so honest, so painfully human that it feels as though it was written by someone sitting in the darkness of modern depression.
Not a prophet calling down fire.
Not a saint standing on a mountaintop.
A suffering man crying from the depths.
And surprisingly, God chose to preserve every word of it.
And it may be the most emotionally devastating chapter in the entire Bible.
Most psalms begin in pain and conclude with praise.
Most psalms eventually arrive at resolution.
Instead, it leaves us sitting in the darkness.
Which is exactly why it matters.
Because sometimes that is where people are.
Sometimes life does not feel victorious.
Sometimes grief stays longer than expected.
And God included Psalm 88 because He already knew that one day His children would need words for the pain they could not explain.
The writer is identified as Heman the Ezrahite.
“O LORD God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee.” (Psalm 88:1)
Even in despair, notice what remains.
He still calls God his salvation.
The word יְשׁוּעָה (yeshuah) means salvation, deliverance, rescue.
It comes from the same Hebrew root connected to the name Yeshua—Jesus.
Before Heman describes his suffering, he anchors himself to the God who saves.
Many Christians wrongly assume that faith means never struggling.
Biblically, faith often means continuing to cry out while struggling.
“For my soul is full of troubles: and my life draweth nigh unto the grave.”
The Hebrew word translated “soul” is נֶפֶשׁ (nephesh).
It refers to the whole inner person.
Heman is saying that every part of him feels overwhelmed.
Many people reading this understand that feeling immediately.
The exhaustion that sleep cannot fix.
The heaviness that rest cannot remove.
The sadness that has no obvious explanation.
The emotional fog that settles over everything.
And what is remarkable is that Scripture does not shame him for saying it.
God allows the lament to remain.
In the inspired pages of His Word.
That alone should comfort countless believers.
The Bible does not pretend suffering isn't real.
The church sometimes pressures people to hide pain.
In fact, when we arrive in the New Testament, we find our Savior entering profound sorrow Himself.
The Greek word περίλυπος (perilupos) means deeply grieved, surrounded by sorrow, distressed beyond ordinary sadness.
The Son of God understands emotional agony.
This is why Christianity offers something no other worldview can offer.
We do not worship a distant God who merely observes suffering.
We worship a Savior who entered it.
“He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.”
Jesus knows what broken hearts feel like.
He knows what despair feels like.
He knows what darkness feels like.
And because He knows, suffering believers never suffer alone.
This is where Psalm 88 becomes astonishingly powerful.
The psalm ends with these words:
Depending on the translation, similar wording appears.
Because God wanted future generations to know something essential.
Your darkest chapter does not disqualify you from His presence.
The existence of Psalm 88 proves that faithful believers can experience overwhelming emotional suffering.
It proves that depression is not automatically evidence of weak faith.
It proves that God hears prayers uttered through tears.
It proves that painful emotions can coexist with genuine trust.
And perhaps most importantly, it proves that God is not frightened by your honesty.
You do not need to perform strength before Him.
You do not need to manufacture happiness.
You do not need to pretend.
You can bring Him the whole truth.
Because the God who inspired Psalm 88 already knows.
And the Savior who walked through Gethsemane already understands.
Yet the story does not end there.
Because while Psalm 88 ends in darkness, the Gospel does not.
The resurrection forever changed how believers understand suffering.
But grief does not write the final chapter.
This is the heartbeat of our message:
The resurrection means that even when we cannot see what God is doing, He is still working.
Even when emotions tell us otherwise, He remains faithful.
Even when the night feels endless, dawn is still coming.
Maybe not as quickly as we wish.
But because Christ rose from the dead, hope remains alive.
If this article found you in a difficult season, do not suffer in silence.
The God of Psalm 88 is still listening.
The Christ of Gethsemane is still near.
And the risen Savior is still transforming lives.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs.
One day you may discover that the chapter you begged God to remove became the chapter He used to reveal how closely He had been carrying you all along.
